title: Analyzing Textual (Mis)Information Shared in WhatsApp Groups
screen_reason: Observational study of all textual messages posted in 364 Brazilian political-oriented public WhatsApp groups during the 2018 election campaign. Messages were matched against claims previously labelled fake by six Brazilian fact-checking sites, giving verbatim numerator and denominator counts (69 distinct misinformation messages out of 37,674 distinct filtered messages; 578 misinformation postings out of 59,979 filtered postings). That is a quantitative share of shared items classified false against an external ground truth, so it meets the SHARING/CONTENT inclusion criterion. The paper's stated aim (comparing linguistic and propagation features) is something else, but the descriptive share is recoverable from the dataset description, which the instructions say to include.

estimates.measure_type: % of textual messages posted (shared) in political WhatsApp groups that carried previously fact-checked false content
estimates.denominator: 59,979 textual messages of more than 180 characters posted in 364 Brazilian political-oriented public WhatsApp groups by 18,725 users, 16 Aug - 7 Oct 2018
estimates.definition: A posting counted in the numerator if its content matched (TF-IDF cosine similarity > 0.4, then manual confirmation) the summary of a claim labelled fake by at least one of six Brazilian fact-checking sites; postings that carried the claim only to refute it (links to fact-checker retractions) were manually excluded.
estimates.misinfo_def: "misinformation, which refers to reportedly false (or inaccurate) information which is often intended to deceive people"

estimates.page_loc: Section 3.2 (p. 228) for the numerator; Section 3.1 (p. 227) and Table 1 (p. 227) for the denominator
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 1,234 claims published during 2018 and labelled fake by at least one of six Brazilian fact-checking sites (Aos fatos; Me engana que eu posto; e-farsas; e ou nao e (G1); Lupa; Boatos.org). Matching by TF-IDF cosine similarity, threshold 0.4 calibrated against manual labelling of a sample of 100 messages ('No match was found in our manual labeling between contents with cosine score below 0.4'); every suspicious message then manually inspected against the fact summaries. No inter-coder reliability statistic reported.

estimates.notes: Value derived per R8 from two verbatim counts sharing the same denominator space (578 misinformation postings; 59,979 filtered postings), not stated as a percentage by the authors. Denominator is restricted to textual messages longer than 180 characters (75% of all messages in these groups are textual; images, videos and audios are excluded from this paper). This is a hard LOWER BOUND on misinformation prevalence by construction: only content already checked by one of six fact-checkers could enter the numerator, and the authors say so explicitly ('We do not claim that there is no misinformation in the unchecked messages'). Groups were discovered by keyword search for chat.whatsapp.com invite links plus a political dictionary (3,444 links found, 1,828 valid), then 364 were joined at random, so the frame is a curated, multi-issue political keyword corpus rather than a platform-random sample.

estimates.notes: DENOMINATOR VARIANT of the first row, not an independent estimate: same corpus, same ground truth, but the unit is the distinct (deduplicated) message rather than the posting. Flagged definition_variant=true so the two are not pooled as two studies. The two numbers differ by a factor of ~5 purely because misinformation messages are reposted far more often than other content (each misinformation message was posted 8.4 times on average vs 1.6 for the corpus as a whole), which is itself one of the paper's findings. Value derived per R8 from verbatim counts with the same denominator.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 'Messages with misinformation have a larger presence of URLs: 50% of the messages with misinformation have at least one URL, whereas only 32% of the other messages contain such links.' Not extracted: the numerator is URL presence, not falsity, so it is not a prevalence estimate (and the 50% is computed inside the misinformation-only subset). (2) All Section 5 propagation statistics ('nearly half of the messages with misinformation were shared more than once, and 20% of them were shared more than 10 times'; '29% and 9% of messages with misinformation and unchecked content' shared at least twice in a group; '83% and 55%' shared in at least two groups; '50% and 20%' shared at least twice) are within-set distributional properties of already-classified messages, not shares of a corpus that are misinformation, so no rows. (3) The paper reports that misinformation is 'concentrated on fewer topics' (Topic 6 almost twice as frequent among misinformation messages), but this is topic concentration read off a histogram, with no top-X%-of-users/sources to Y%-of-activity pair, so it fails R1 and is not a CONCENTRATION row. (4) 'textual messages comprise the great majority on these groups, representing 75% of all messages shared' is a media-type share, not a misinformation share. (5) Neither of the two extracted percentages is printed in the paper; both are exact part/whole shares of verbatim counts (R8). An adjudicator who reads R8 strictly as 'verbatim percentages only' would drop both rows and mark this paper as counts-only. (6) QUOTE MECHANICS: this is a two-column ACM PDF and the text rendering interleaves the two columns on every line, with no reading-order rendering available, so no sentence spanning a line break is contiguous in the text file. source_quote therefore holds the longest strictly contiguous span carrying the value (the numerator), and the denominator sentence is given in the denominator/n fields and, for the second row, in moderator_quote; the rob quotes are the same sentences reflowed across the column wrap ('misin-/formation' rejoined).

rob.design: Observational digital-trace study. Frame: public WhatsApp groups found by searching Google/Twitter/Facebook for 'chat.whatsapp.com' invite links combined with a 2018 Brazilian election dictionary (3,444 distinct links found, 1,828 valid), of which 364 were joined at random using three phones; all content posted 16 Aug - 7 Oct 2018 was collected via WebWhatsAppAPI (591,162 messages, 18,725 users, phone numbers anonymised). Analysis restricted to textual messages > 180 characters (59,979 postings; 37,674 distinct after collapsing near-duplicates at Jaccard > 0.7). Misinformation identified by TF-IDF cosine similarity to 1,234 fake-labelled fact-check summaries from six Brazilian fact-checkers, threshold 0.4 set by comparison with manual labelling of 100 messages, followed by manual inspection of every suspicious message and manual removal of debunking/retraction posts. No response rate applies; no inter-coder agreement statistic reported; the misinformation set is bounded by fact-checker coverage, which the authors acknowledge.
rob.item6_quote: We here are particularly interested in the spread of misinformation, which refers to reportedly false (or inaccurate) information which is often intended to deceive people.
rob.item10_quote: This process led to the identification of 69 distinct textual messages containing previously checked misinformation. These messages were shared 578 times in our dataset.
